overview: Memeware 7.3's FastPlace is a one-statement module: on every UpdateEvent it writes mc.rightClickDelayTimer = 0. Vanilla sets that timer to 4 at the top of rightClickMouse(), decrements it once per tick, and only calls rightClickMouse() for a held use key while the timer reads exactly 0, so a held right click fires at most 5 actions per second. Pinning the timer to zero makes the gate pass on every tick, lifting the placement rate toward the 20/s tick ceiling. The module is a pure client-side timing hack: it changes no packet contents and sends nothing of its own, and its only server-visible fingerprint is the denser stream of C08 placement packets the accelerated clicks produce.

sections.p: The whole module is a single @Handler-flagged Consumer field on the lwjeb event bus, registered in the constructor (super("Fast Place", 0, Category.MISC)) with no settings, no enable/disable logic and no mode gating. The lambda executes on every UpdateEvent and contains exactly one statement: mc.rightClickDelayTimer = 0. Because UpdateEvent fires once per client tick, the assignment runs 20 times per second, so the one-per-tick decrement the run loop applies to the timer (Minecraft.java line 1452) is undone before the next input poll and the field never leaves zero while the module is on.

Two touchpoints in Minecraft.java define the cheat. rightClickMouse() opens by writing rightClickDelayTimer = 4 (line 1326), which is the cooldown: one action, then a 4-tick wait. The run-tick input section decrements the timer once per tick (lines 1452-1453) and only invokes rightClickMouse() for a held use key when the timer is exactly 0 and the player is not already using an item (line 1790). The result is a 200ms action grid, 5 per second. Zeroing the timer removes the cooldown while leaving the isUsingItem guard intact, so the module cannot double-fire inside an active item-use animation; it only eliminates the inter-action wait, which is what pushes sustained placements to the 20/s tick rate.

For block placement the accelerated clicks become a denser C08PacketPlayerBlockPlacement stream: a spam clicker places up to 20 blocks per second with full coordinates and facing instead of vanilla's 5, and every placement is a legitimate-looking packet. The same gate governs item use, so the module also speeds up soup and food consumption and bow re-pulls on servers that only police the right-click cadence. The module never touches the C08 payload, so the only fingerprints are timing: the inter-placement interval collapses from a 200ms grid to a sub-50ms scatter, which is precisely the signal placement-rate checks are built around.

files.label: FastPlace.java (module logic)
files.explanation: The file is the module body: the constructor registers the module under Category.MISC with key 0, and the public @Handler-flagged Consumer field eventConsumer0 carries the lambda that zeroes mc.rightClickDelayTimer. The @Handler marker is what the lwjeb bus scans at registration time, so the field's accept() runs on every UpdateEvent with no further dispatch code; there is nothing else in the class to read.

files.label: Minecraft.java (the timer being zeroed)
files.explanation: The three rightClickDelayTimer touchpoints that define the gate the module defeats. rightClickMouse() writes 4 at line 1326, the run-tick loop decrements at lines 1452-1453, and the held-use branch at line 1790 requires the timer to read exactly 0 before calling rightClickMouse(). The module's write lands between the decrement and the poll, so the gate always passes and each tick may fire a new right-click action.

countering.label: FastPlace (placement-rate window)
countering.explanation: NCP's blockplace FastPlace scores every real placement into data.fastPlaceBuckets, an ActionFrequency(2, 1000) pair of half-second buckets (BlockPlaceData line 53), plus a short-term tick counter. The window score fullScore = fastPlaceBuckets.score(1f) is compared against cc.fastPlaceLimit, default 15 per second (DefaultConfig line 184), and the short-term window flags more than fastPlaceShortTermLimit (6) placements inside fastPlaceShortTermTicks (10) ticks (lines 59-89). Vanilla caps at 5 placements per second, so a legitimate player never approaches either bound, while the module's zeroed delay pushes sustained placement toward 20/s and trips the window limit with cancel actions from vl>5. The check fires only from the Bukkit BlockPlaceEvent path, so the accelerated item-use C08s (facing 255, air coordinates) the same gate produces never reach it; the pressure lands on real block placements only.

countering.label: Direction (facing validation)
countering.explanation: Direction extends AbstractBlockDirectionCheck and scores the angular distance between the placement's claimed facing and the player's actual look direction, accumulating blockplace VL through addVL with a per-hit cooldown. The module itself sends honest facings, so a single placement is not a fingerprint; the check matters as the companion to the rate check because a placement stream that must also track a moving cursor (strafing scaffold-style placements) forces look updates that lag the placement packets, and the sustained mismatch is what accumulates. Standing-still fast place is invisible to it, which is why the rate window does the real work.

countering.label: BlockPlace packet listener (soup auto-heal only)
countering.explanation: Arc v2's BLOCK_PLACE packet adapter (lines 134-142) only inspects the held item and reacts when it is MUSHROOM_SOUP, feeding the AUTO_HEAL check; there is no placement-rate, direction or placement-reach validation anywhere in its check tree. The accelerated C08 stream from this module therefore passes Arc v2's block-place layer untouched, and the real pressure on Arc v2 comes from its movement layer (MorePackets max-packets 30/s with kick at 70/s, Flight) rather than from any placement check. This is a gap entry: the AC's block-place surface does not counter the module at all.
